name: Precision bias
statement: A number stated precisely is treated as better founded than a round one, so precise offers and anchors move other people's numbers further.
meaning: Two claims travel under this name and only one of them has been measured. The broad claim is that precision implies accuracy, so a figure given to the decimal place is nearer the truth than a rounded one. No study of a construct by the name 'precision bias' was located in these searches. The narrow claim does have a literature, under the names anchor precision and the price precision effect. It says that a number expressed precisely exerts more pull on somebody else's number than a round number of the same size. Janiszewski and Uy put the mechanism in the arithmetic. Their abstract argues that a precise anchor is represented on a subjective scale with a finer resolution, so each mental step away from it is smaller and the total correction is smaller. Mason, Lee, Wiley and Ames put it in the social inference instead. A negotiator who opens at $4,885 seems to have worked something out, and one who opens at $5,000 seems to have guessed. The two accounts agree on the direction and disagree about who the effect should fail for.

origin.note: No publication coining the phrase 'precision bias' was located. Janiszewski and Uy's five studies are the root of the effect the phrase is applied to, and their paper does not use the phrase in its title or abstract. Wikipedia's article opens by calling precision bias a cognitive bias and cites for that a page range in the proceedings of the 2011 Cognitive Science Society meeting, given with no title and no authors.

evidence:
Mason, Lee, Wiley and Ames ran six studies on first offers. Studies 1a to 1d were vignettes: recipients of a round offer adjusted further in their counteroffer than recipients of a precise offer of similar size. Adjustments were $9.53 against $7.94 and $8.39 on a $20 jewellery offer, $2.56 against $1.77 and $2.19 on a $10 coffee contract, $4.36 against $3.15 and $3.85 on a $10 restaurant contract, and $10.56 against $7.19 and $8.08 on a $20 textbook. Partial eta squared on the round against precise contrast ran from .030 to .073. The restaurant study is the weak one. Its main effect was marginal, F(2, 82) = 3.04, p = .053, and its 85 participants were managers and MBAs rather than the MTurk workers used in the other three. Study 2 put 130 buyer-seller dyads of managers, MBAs and undergraduates through a live car negotiation. Sellers facing a precise opening offer countered $3,197 away from it against $4,235 for round openings, t(69) = 2.39, p = .020, d = .57. The gap in adjustment survived to the settlement, at $2,256 against $2,963, t(69) = 2.043, p = .045, d = .49. The settlement prices themselves did not differ, $12,932 against $13,022, p = .34, because buyers told to be precise also opened lower. Study 3 gave 238 MTurk sellers a $2,000, $1,865 or $2,135 offer for a used car and measured whether the buyer seemed to have researched the price. Precision raised that rating, the rating predicted smaller adjustments, and the indirect effect had a 95% bias-corrected bootstrap interval of 3.49 to 40.68.

The authors also counted how offers are actually phrased. Of 356 opening offers made by 113 executives and 243 MBA students in class exercises, 48% carried a single significant digit, 49% carried two, and none was specified to the dollar. Of 1,511 Zillow listings in four American cities, 73% of homes between $10,000 and $99,999 ended in at least three zeros, as did 98% of homes between $1m and $10m.

The effect has been found on prices as well as offers. Thomas, Simon and Kadiyali report five studies in which buyers underestimate the magnitude of precise prices. Their participants judged $395,425 to be smaller than $395,000; a nationally representative sample of homeowners was willing to pay more for houses priced at $364,578 than at $365,000; and buyers in two residential property markets paid higher sale prices where list prices were more precise. Those figures come from the paper's abstract, which was the only part obtained.

Hukkanen and Keloharju looked at 1,889 initial all-cash takeover bids for listed American targets announced between 1985 and 2015. About 14% were priced to the nearest five dollars a share and almost half to the nearest dollar, with 18% finer than a quarter. Bids at five-dollar precision moved 16% on average from opening to final price, against 5% for bids finer than a quarter. A bid finer than a quarter was 9% more likely to close than a five-dollar bid and 6% more likely than a one-dollar bid. On the median transaction the round pricing is worth about four million dollars more paid for the target. The authors looked for four ways a precise bidder might pay for that advantage, including a worse announcement return, and found none.

examples.tag: The asking price with digits in it
examples.text: A flat listed at 364,578 pounds and a flat listed at 365,000 invite different counteroffers. The precise figure reads as the output of a calculation, and buyers move less far from it when they name their own number.

A quote of 8,432 pounds is taken as the result of somebody adding things up. A quote of 8,500 is taken as a figure somebody settled on. Both may be equally accurate, and the first pulls the negotiation further towards itself.

A candidate who asks for 52,750 pounds sets a different conversation from one who asks for 52,000. The precise figure implies a worked-out case sitting behind it, so the employer's counteroffer starts nearer to where it began.

replication.headline: A preregistered study of 400 estate agents reproduced the negotiation effect, and three experiments with 1,505 Danes found no precision effect on trust in official numbers.
replication.detail:
Frech, Loschelder and Friese preregistered a field experiment with 400 professional real-estate agents, who negotiated over a house inside their expertise or a motor yacht outside it. Their abstract reports that they replicated the advantageous anchor precision effect, that too much precision backfired in both domains, and that the effect ran through competence attributed to the opponent. It is a replication of Loschelder, Friese, Schaerer and Galinsky, whose five experiments covered 1,320 experts and amateurs in real-estate, jewellery, car and human-resources negotiations. That paper's abstract reports positive linear effects of precision for amateurs and inverted-U effects for experts, with the downturn removed when the first mover justified the number. Both are quoted here from their abstracts at PubMed.

Schultze and Loschelder moved the question to advice taking, preregistered, with 195 students estimating the lengths of 30 rivers. Advisers gave moderate, high or extreme precision, and the advice taking score rose from 0.34 to 0.41 to 0.42, F(2, 388) = 27.26, p < .001, eta squared = .03. Extreme precision did not backfire, even when the advice read 3,461.73 km. The authors treat the pattern as a monotone increase that flattens rather than an inverted U.

Olsen found nothing in a political setting. Three experiments were embedded in one YouGov survey of 1,505 Danes. The first asked which of two economic forecasts they trusted, and ran each topic twice, once with the precise figure set below the round one and once above it. Round won where the precise figure was higher: 76.4% took a 1.5% growth rate over 1.537%, and 57.7% took a 20bn kroner deficit over 20.37bn. Precise won where it was lower: 72.8% took the precise unemployment figure, and 51.6% the precise growth rate, a split within noise. Olsen reads the pattern as a preference for the gloomier number rather than for the rounder one. Asked to rate confidence in single numbers, they gave 4.7 to both the precise and the round budget figure, 3.8 to both unemployment figures, and more to the round growth rate than the precise one, 5.2 against 4.8, t(754) = 2.5, p = .013. Of the three long-term policy goals in the third experiment, only public expenditure showed a precision effect, F(1, 1501) = 8.42, p < .01, and Olsen notes that the accompanying frame manipulation moved nothing, which he treats as a reason for caution. His summary is that no clear evidence of a precision effect appeared in politics.

study.cite: Frech, M.-L., Loschelder, D. D., & Friese, M. (2019). How and why different forms of expertise moderate anchor precision in price decisions: A pre-registered field experiment. Experimental Psychology, 66(2), 165-175.

limits:
The largest meta-analysis of anchoring declined to test this moderator. Roseler and Schutz pooled 393 effect sizes from 17,708 participants and report anchoring at g = 0.689, 95% CI 0.589 to 0.789. They coded anchor precision by whether the last digit was zero, found that anchors close to the true value were being coded precise more often, and write that they therefore chose not to analyse precision. So the pooled evidence on anchoring says nothing either way about this claim, and the entry rests on individual studies.

The effect is not uniform in size or sign. Loschelder and colleagues report it reversing above a point for experts, Olsen reports its absence across three political experiments, and Schultze and Loschelder report a small one, eta squared of .03, that stops rising rather than reversing. Mason and colleagues' four vignette studies ran on 280, 257, 85 and 247 people answering hypothetical questions about jewellery, coffee, a restaurant contract and a textbook. Three of those were MTurk samples. The 85 were managers and MBAs, and theirs is the study whose main effect was marginal.

Hukkanen and Keloharju's takeover results are associations in observational data and the authors present them as such. Their figures here are read from the accepted version of the Financial Management article, dated 12 January 2018 and posted by Aalto University. The Harvard Business School working paper of 2 November 2015 covers 1,769 bids to 2012 rather than 1,889 to 2015, and reports somewhat larger effects. Its finding that round bidders also suffer a worse announcement return did not survive into the published version, which reports no such penalty.

Several papers could not be read, though not for the reason a paywall would give. Janiszewski and Uy, Loschelder and colleagues and Jerez-Fernandez and colleagues sit at SAGE, Frech and colleagues at Hogrefe, and Thomas and colleagues at INFORMS. Each of those hosts answered on 21 September 2026 with a Cloudflare bot challenge, to a browser-like fetcher and a plain one alike, rather than with a subscription notice. Their abstracts at PubMed and Crossref are used here instead. Jerez-Fernandez, Angulo and Oppenheimer, the paper Wikipedia leans on hardest, carries no abstract at PubMed. Princeton's DataSpace holds the 2012 senior thesis behind it, guarded by a proof-of-work challenge that was solved here, and the record turns out to hold no file and to offer a reading room copy at Mudd Library instead. Nothing from that paper is reported here as a finding. Searches for the term itself covered Crossref title and bibliographic queries, PubMed and web search on 21 September 2026; OpenAlex again returned a rate-limit error. Crossref and PubMed hits on the exact phrase are about measurement error in chemistry, radiocarbon dating, clinical assays and animal behaviour scoring.
misreadings:
The name is the first thing to get wrong. Precision bias is a term of bias catalogues rather than of research psychology, and the studies behind it were published under other names: anchor precision, the price precision effect, the too-much-precision effect. An entry that treats it as a single measured construct is describing a heading rather than a finding, in the way the affinity-bias entry here, no. 273, describes one.

Wikipedia's article, the main source of the popular version, contains three attributions its cited papers do not support. It credits Janiszewski and Uy with an analysis of 12,581 Florida home sales; their abstract describes five studies of adjustment away from anchors, and the analysis of residential property transactions belongs to Thomas, Simon and Kadiyali's Study 5. It says Mason and colleagues found precise offers reduced the likelihood of a counteroffer being made at all; that paper, read in full here, measures the size of counteroffers and the final settlement price and reports no such measure. It cites Peters, Markowitz, Nadratowski and Shoots-Reinhard on climate posts as evidence about precision. Their experiment contrasts posts describing consequences with an Arabic integer, such as 90%, against posts using verbal terms such as 'almost all', and their two observational studies turn on whether a post carries any integer at all. The comparison is between numbers and words, not between precise and round numbers.

The effect is a moderator of anchoring, not a rival to it. Anchoring says the number pulls; precision says a finer-grained number pulls harder. Anchoring has its own entry here, no. 6, and its evidence is far stronger than the precision evidence.

It is also not the 99-ending price. Charm pricing turns on the leading digit changing between $3.99 and $4.00, and it sits here under psychological pricing, no. 107, with its own meta-analysis. The precision claim concerns numbers of the same leading digits differing in how many of the trailing ones are zero, such as $364,578 against $365,000.

The practical advice usually drawn from it runs past the evidence. Mason and colleagues say plainly that they did not test the risks, and list two: that an overly precise offer might signal inflexibility and cause avoidable impasses, and that it could be read as a manipulative gambit. Loschelder and colleagues then found the second of those happening with experts. Olsen found that a Danish electorate trusted the round growth forecast more than the precise one.
